parsed.claim: Potential IDOR on orders endpoint based on a single request returning a 200 status with a response different from baseline.
coverage_gaps: Multi-user authorization boundary testing (own orders vs. other users' orders)
Unauthenticated access attempt to the endpoint
Different order_id ranges or formats (sequential IDs, UUIDs, negative numbers, zero)
Role-based access control testing (customer, admin, guest roles across different orders)
Response payload comparison: sensitive fields vs. expected fields per authorization level
Reproducibility validation: repeated requests to confirm the variance is not random
parsed.deception_check: The operator observed a 200 response that differed from a vague baseline and attributed it to a vulnerability without testing whether the difference represents actual unauthorized access or merely normal response variance (user state, timestamps, logging, etc.).

objections.concern: Claim lacks specificity: 'response looked different' is not falsifiable or reproducible. No details on endpoint path, order ID tested, authorization context, or specific fields that differed.
objections.evidence_request: Provide exact endpoint, HTTP method, request parameters (especially order_id and any auth headers), and a detailed breakdown of what fields/values differed from baseline. Include a screenshot or response dump.

objections.concern: Single-request testing is insufficient for IDOR validation. IDOR requires proof of boundary crossing across multiple authorization contexts.
objections.evidence_request: Test the same order_id across at least three scenarios: (1) authenticated as the owner, (2) authenticated as a different user, (3) unauthenticated. Compare the response content in each case. Reproduce the 'different' response at least 5 times to rule out variance.

objections.concern: No evidence of unauthorized data access. HTTP 200 is a normal success response; the vulnerability claim hinges on whether sensitive data was returned, not the status code.
objections.evidence_request: Analyze the response content: does it contain order details (items, amounts, shipping address, customer name, etc.) that the requesting user should NOT have access to? Compare against what the same user sees for their own orders. Establish a control.

objections.concern: Baseline comparison is undefined. 'Different from baseline' is meaningless without specifying what the baseline is (same endpoint with your own order_id? A reference request? An older response?).
objections.evidence_request: Define the baseline explicitly. For example: 'baseline is a 200 response with fields [X, Y, Z] when requesting my own order; the test returned [X, Y, Z, sensitive_field].'

parsed.one_more_thread:
If you had one more hour: dump both responses (baseline and 'different') side-by-side. Parse every field. Cross-reference against: (1) what your own order returns when you request it, (2) what a peer account's order returns when you request it, (3) what that endpoint returns when you're unauthenticated. Only after this control establish a clear authorization boundary crossing. IDOR isn't "response was different"—it's "I accessed data I shouldn't have access to." Prove the latter.</thinking>
